entry: Alcoholic drink brewed from fermented [[Cereal|cereal]] grain, most commonly malted [[Barley|barley]]. The grain is mashed to convert its starch to sugars, which dissolve in water to form wort. [[Yeast|Yeast]] ferments the wort into [[Ethanol|ethanol]] and carbonation. Most modern beer is brewed with [[Hops|hops]], which add bitterness and act as a natural preservative. Wheat, maize, rice, and oats are also used. Beer is one of the oldest and most widely consumed alcoholic drinks. Residues of beer with the consistency of gruel, about 13,000 years old, were found at Raqefet Cave near [[Haifa]] in northern Israel, and the [[Code of Hammurabi]] (1750 BC) included laws regulating it. Beer usually contains about 4% to 6% alcohol by volume (ABV). Brewing is a global business, dominated by several multinational corporations alongside thousands of smaller producers. Beer can cause health problems if consumed often or in excess, and alcohol is classed as a Group 1 carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer.

[[Insect|Insect]] of the order Coleoptera, the largest of all insect orders. Beetles have hardened front wings, or elytra, that form protective wing-cases, and they undergo complete [[Metamorphosis|metamorphosis]] through a relatively immobile [[Pupa|pupal]] stage. Roughly 400,000 species have been described, almost 40% of described [[Arthropod|arthropods]] and 25% of all known animal species, and total species estimates range from 0.9 million to 2.1 million. Beetles live in almost every habitat except the sea and the polar regions. Many feed on plants, fungi, and debris, and some eat other invertebrates. Serious pests include the [[Weevil|boll weevil]] of cotton and the Colorado potato beetle, while [[Coccinellidae|ladybirds]] eat [[Aphid|aphids]] and other crop-damaging insects. Over 300 species are used as food, mostly as larvae. The sacred scarabs of [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egypt]] were beetles, and the scientific study of beetles is called coleopterology.

Edible taproot of *Beta vulgaris* subsp. *vulgaris*, a root vegetable also called table beet or garden beet. Its leaves, known as beet greens, are eaten as a leaf vegetable. Beetroot is native to the [[Azores]], Western Europe to the Mediterranean, and [[India]]. It can be eaten raw, roasted, steamed, or boiled, and it is often [[Pickling|pickled]]. Sliced pickled beetroot is a common ingredient in traditional [[Hamburger|hamburgers]] in Australia and New Zealand, and beetroot soup, such as [[Borscht]], is common in Eastern Europe. The plant was domesticated in the ancient Middle East, primarily for its greens, and was grown by the Ancient Egyptians, Greeks, and Romans. From the [[Middle Ages]], beetroot was used to treat digestive and blood illnesses. In the mid-17th century, wine was often colored with beetroot juice. Beetroot was grown in many victory gardens during [[World War II]].

Suite of behavioral and cognitive traits associated with [[Human|humans]] (*Homo sapiens*), including abstract and symbolic thought, planning depth, cumulative culture, and complex social learning. These traits are inferred from symbolic artifacts, ritualized behavior, music and dance, sophisticated hunting strategies, and advanced stone technologies. It is best understood as a mosaic of traits that emerged gradually and were expressed unevenly across time and populations. Anatomically modern humans had the necessary neural architecture by at least about 300,000 years ago, but symbolic artifacts appear sporadically in Africa between about 150,000 and 75,000 years ago and became widespread only after populations grew denser. The late [[Upper Paleolithic]] model places an abrupt cognitive change in Africa about 40,000–50,000 years ago, while gradualist models locate it earlier, in the African Middle Stone Age. It has been argued that climatic conditions of the [[Last Glacial Period]], causing [[Population bottleneck|population bottlenecks]], contributed to the success of *Homo sapiens* over [[Neanderthal|Neanderthals]] and [[Denisovan|Denisovans]].

Systematic approach to the study of behavior in humans and other animals. It assumes that behavior is either a reflex elicited by antecedent stimuli or a consequence of an individual's history of reinforcement and punishment. Behaviorism emerged in the early 1900s as a reaction to depth psychology and other traditional psychology, which had difficulty making testable predictions. [[Edward Thorndike|Thorndike]] pioneered the law of effect in the late 19th century, and in 1924 [[John B. Watson|John B. Watson]] devised methodological behaviorism, which rejected introspective methods. In 1945 [[B. F. Skinner|B. F. Skinner]] proposed radical behaviorism, arguing that covert events such as cognition and emotion are subject to the same controlling variables as observable behavior. Skinner's analysis of reinforcement became known as operant conditioning, while [[Ivan Pavlov|Pavlov]] studied conditioned reflexes. The late 20th-century cognitive revolution largely replaced behaviorism as an explanatory theory with [[Cognitive psychology|cognitive psychology]]. Applied behavior analysis treats developmental conditions such as [[Autism|autism]], and cognitive-behavioral therapies have proved useful for [[Phobia|simple phobias]], PTSD, and mood disorders.

Beast in the biblical Book of Job, an echo of primeval chaos monsters created by God. Its Hebrew name has the same form as the plural of the word for "beast," suggesting an augmentative sense of "great beast." In Jewish apocrypha, Behemoth is an unconquerable land-monster living east of the [[Garden of Eden]], and it is paired with the sea-monster [[Leviathan]] in later texts. Behemoth has been widely identified with the [[Hippopotamus|hippopotamus]]. Metaphorically, the name is used for any extremely large or powerful entity.

International airport in [[Beijing]], [[China]], and the busier of the city's two international airports. It lies 32 km (20 mi) northeast of downtown Beijing, in suburban Shunyi. The airport opened on March 1, 1958,. Its IATA code, PEK, is based on the city's former romanized name, Peking. Terminal 3, completed in February 2008 for the Beijing Summer Olympics, was the largest airport passenger terminal in the world by floor area when it opened. In 2013 the airport handled 83.7 million passengers, making it the second-busiest airport in the world that year.

Capital and largest city of [[Lebanon]], on a peninsula at the midpoint of the country's Mediterranean coast. Beirut has been inhabited for more than 5,000 years, making it one of the oldest cities in the world. Its name derives from a [[Phoenicia|Phoenician]] word meaning "wells," a reference to the site's accessible water table. Greater Beirut had a population of 2.4 million as of 2025, just under half of Lebanon's population. The city is the seat of government, a center of banking and corporate activity, and an important seaport. Beirut was severely damaged by the [[Lebanese Civil War]], the 2006 Lebanon War, and the 2020 explosion in the Port of Beirut, and it was rebuilt after each event. Excavations have uncovered Phoenician, Hellenistic, Roman, Byzantine, Arab, Crusader, Persian, and Ottoman remains.

Capital and largest city of Pará state in northern [[Brazil]]. Belém is the gateway to the [[Amazon River|Amazon River]], with a busy port, airport, and bus station. It lies about 100 km (62.1 mi) upriver from the [[Atlantic Ocean]] on the Pará River. Its estimated population is 1,398,531, or 2,491,052 with its metropolitan area, the 12th most populous city in Brazil. Founded in 1616 by the Kingdom of [[Portugal]], it was the first European colony on the Amazon but did not become part of Brazil until 1775. The name is Portuguese for Bethlehem, and the city is also known as the Cidade das Mangueiras, or City of [[Mango|Mango]] Trees.

Hungarian-American actor best known for playing [[Count Dracula]] in *Dracula* (1931). Born Béla Ferenc Dezső Blaskó, he began acting on the Hungarian stage in 1901 and later emigrated to the United States. He played Dracula on Broadway in 1927, and the 1931 film version, produced by [[Universal Pictures]], made him a horror icon. Typecasting limited his roles, though he co-starred with [[Boris Karloff]] in several horror films. He became addicted to doctor-prescribed morphine and methadone, and after 1948 his career declined; his later films were mostly low-budget productions.

Landlocked country in Eastern Europe. It is bordered by [[Russia]] to the east, [[Ukraine]] to the south, [[Poland]] to the west, and [[Lithuania]] and [[Latvia]] to the northwest. Its area is 207,600 sq km (80,200 sq mi), and its population is 9.1 million. [[Minsk]] is the capital and largest city. In 1945 the Byelorussian SSR became a founding member of the [[United Nations]], along with the [[Soviet Union]]. The parliament proclaimed sovereignty on July 27, 1990, and Belarus gained independence on August 25, 1991. Alexander Lukashenko was elected president in the country's first and only free election after independence and has served ever since. Critics describe his government as authoritarian and centralized, and Belarus ranks low in international measurements of press freedom and civil liberties. Belarus is the only European country that continues to use capital punishment.

Capital, largest city, and main port of [[Northern Ireland]]. It stands on the River Lagan and is connected to the open sea through Belfast Lough and the North Channel. Chartered as an English settlement in 1613, the town grew with an influx of Scottish Presbyterians. It was granted city status in 1888, when it was the world's largest center of [[Linen|linen]] manufacture, and by the 1900s its shipyards were building up to a quarter of all United Kingdom tonnage. Sectarian tensions erupted into violence in 1920–22 and during [[The Troubles|the Troubles]] of the late 1960s to 1990s. Since the [[Good Friday Agreement]], the electoral balance has shifted toward Irish nationalists, albeit with no overall majority. Belfast has two universities, and since 2021 it has been a [[UNESCO]]-designated City of Music.

Parliamentary constitutional monarchy in northwestern Europe. It covers 30,689 sq km (11,849 sq mi), and its population is more than 11.8 million. The capital, [[Brussels]], is the de facto capital of the [[European Union]] and hosts the headquarters of [[NATO]]. Belgium borders the [[Netherlands]], [[Luxembourg]], and [[France]], and its three regions are [[Flanders]], [[Wallonia]], and the Brussels-Capital Region. Its complex federal system reflects divisions between Dutch and French speakers, and a record 589 days passed without government formation after the 2010 federal election. Belgium was the first country in continental Europe to industrialize, and it became independent in 1830 after the Belgian Revolution. Centuries of contests among European powers earned it the moniker "the Battlefield of Europe".

Capital and largest city of [[Serbia]], at the confluence of the Sava and [[Danube]] rivers. The city proper had a population of 1,197,114 at the 2022 census, and its administrative area totaled 1,682,720. Belgrade is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Europe, and it was conquered by the [[Ottoman Empire]] in 1521. It was the capital of [[Yugoslavia]] from its creation until its dissolution. Belgrade is the seat of the central government and home to almost all of Serbia's largest companies, media, and scientific institutions. It hosted the first [[Non-Aligned Movement]] summit in 1961 and the [[Eurovision Song Contest]] in 2008. In a strategic position, the city has been battled over in 115 wars and razed 44 times.

Country on the northeastern coast of [[Central America]], and part of the Caribbean region. [[Mexico]] lies to the north, [[Guatemala]] to the west and south, and the [[Caribbean Sea]] to the east. Belize is a member of the Caribbean Community (CARICOM). The [[Maya civilization]] spread into the area between 1500 BC and 300 AD and flourished until about 1200. Belize became a British colony in 1840 and was known as British Honduras until 1973. It became independent from the [[United Kingdom]] on September 21, 1981, and it is the only mainland Central American Commonwealth realm, with King Charles III as head of state. Its population is 397,483 (2022), and English is the only official language in Central America. Its capital is Belmopan, and its largest city is Belize City.

Directly struck idiophone, usually a hollow cup that vibrates in a single strong tone when struck. Bells are usually cast from [[Bronze|bell metal]], a type of bronze, though small ornamental bells may be made of glass, ceramic, or pressed metal. A bell is struck by an internal clapper, an external hammer, or, in small bells, a loose sphere as in a jingle bell. Bells hang singly in towers or form ensembles such as carillons, and many public buildings house [[Clock|clock]] bells. Historically, bells have been associated with religious rites and have commemorated important events. The earliest archaeological evidence dates from the 3rd millennium BC in the Yangshao culture of Neolithic China. By the 13th century BC, bells over 150 kilograms (330 pounds) were being cast in China. After AD 1000, [[Iron|iron]] became the most commonly used metal for bells instead of bronze.

Research and development company headquartered in Murray Hill, [[New Jersey]]. Originating in the late 19th century as the Western Electric Engineering Department, it was reformed as Bell Telephone Laboratories in 1925. Its researchers are credited with the [[Transistor|transistor]], the [[Laser|laser]], the [[Charge-coupled device|charge-coupled device]], information theory, and the [[Unix]] operating system, as well as the programming languages [[C (programming language)|C]] and [[C++]]. Eleven [[Nobel Prize|Nobel Prizes]] and five Turing Awards have been awarded for work completed at Bell Laboratories. The company, formerly a subsidiary of the American Telephone and Telegraph Company (AT&T), is owned by the Finnish company Nokia.

Fruit of plants in the Grossum Group of *Capsicum annuum*. Bell peppers are sweet, non-pungent cultivars that are botanically berries but are commonly used as a vegetable, in [[Salad|salads]] and as [[Pizza|pizza]] toppings. They come in red, yellow, orange, green, white, and purple, and unripe fruit is usually green. Red bell peppers are simply ripened green peppers. A 100-gram reference amount of raw red bell pepper supplies 26 calories and 158% of the Daily Value (DV) for vitamin C. Peppers are native to [[Mexico]], [[Central America]], the Caribbean, and northern South America. Seeds were imported to [[Spain]] in 1493 and then spread through Europe and Asia. Bell peppers and other cultivars of *C. annuum* are used to produce [[Paprika]].

Facial paralysis that causes a temporary inability to control the facial muscles on one side of the face. It results from dysfunction of cranial nerve VII, the facial nerve, and many believe it is due to a viral infection; the cause is unknown in most cases. Risk factors include [[Diabetes|diabetes]], a recent upper respiratory tract infection, and [[Pregnancy|pregnancy]]. It is the most common cause of one-sided facial nerve paralysis, accounting for about 70% of cases. Most cases improve within weeks, and complete recovery usually occurs within six months. Corticosteroids improve outcomes, but surgery is generally not recommended.

Physics theorem on the incompatibility of [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]] with local hidden-variable theories. John Stewart Bell introduced the first such result in 1964, building on the Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen paradox about [[Quantum entanglement|quantum entanglement]]. Bell showed that quantum physics predicts correlations that violate a constraint now called a Bell inequality. The first laboratory experiment to observe such a violation was conducted by John Clauser and Stuart Freedman and published in 1970. Later Bell tests, many aimed at closing loopholes, have consistently found that physical systems obey quantum mechanics and violate Bell inequalities. Interpretations of quantum mechanics disagree about what the theorem implies.

American fashion [[Model (person)|model]]. Hadid began modeling at age 16 and signed with IMG Models in August 2014. In 2016 she was voted Model of the Year by industry professionals for Models.com. In 2017 she broke the record for the most [[Vogue (magazine)|Vogue]] September covers in one year, appearing in five international editions. The British Fashion Council named her Model of the Year in 2022, and [[Time (magazine)|Time]] listed her among the 100 most influential people in the world in 2023. As of 2023 she was one of the world's highest paid models, earning $19 million.

Period of French and European history from the end of the [[Franco-Prussian War]] in 1871 to the outbreak of [[World War I]] in 1914. It occurred during the Third French Republic and was characterized by optimism, regional peace, economic prosperity, nationalism, colonial expansion, and technological, scientific, and cultural innovation. The arts flourished, particularly in [[Paris]]. The label was applied in retrospect, when the era was seen as a continental European "Golden Age" in contrast to the violence of the [[Napoleonic Wars]] and World War I. Prosperity did not reach all, and a large [[Underclass|underclass]] saw little of its wonders.

European plant species in the family [[Asteraceae]], often considered the archetypal daisy. Known as the common or lawn daisy, *Bellis perennis* is a perennial herb about 20 cm (8 in) tall with rosettes of small, spoon-shaped leaves. It blooms from March to September, and its flower heads have white ray florets, often tipped red, around yellow disc florets; the flowers follow the position of the sun. The species colonizes lawns and is difficult to eradicate by mowing. It is native to western, central, and northern Europe and is naturalized in most temperate regions. Its young leaves can be eaten, and its flower buds and petals appear in [[Sandwich|sandwiches]], soups, and salads. The name "daisy" may derive from "day's eye," because the flower head closes at night.

Middle Eastern dance that originated in [[Egypt]] and features movements of the hips and torso. It is also called Middle Eastern or Arabic dance, a Western-coined exonym; the Arabic name is raqs sharqi, or "oriental dance." Belly dance is primarily torso-driven, with an emphasis on isolations of the torso muscles rather than movements of the limbs through space. Its movements include percussive hip accents and fluid figures of eight. Egyptian styles and costumes are the most recognized worldwide because of Egyptian cinema. The term translates the French danse du ventre and was first used in English by Charles James Wills in 1883.

Capital and largest city of the Brazilian state of [[Minas Gerais]]. It is the sixth-most-populous city in [[Brazil]], with a population of around 2.4 million, and its metropolitan area has about 6 million people. It was planned and built in the 1890s to replace Ouro Preto as the state capital, and it is the first planned modern city in Brazil. Its planners, Aarão Reis and Francisco Bicalho, drew inspiration from Washington, D.C. The city is known for the Pampulha Complex, an early modernist work by [[Oscar Niemeyer]] that received [[UNESCO]] World Heritage status in 2016. Belo Horizonte was one of the host cities of the 1950 and 2014 [[FIFA]] World Cup.
